content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a stereo matching method based on existing baseline architectures, with two additions: first the authors propose matching based on canny edge detection and second a network module to improve stereo matching by convolving on image features and disparity. Experiments show that a small improvement can be obtained by using edge-based matching constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The paper to a large part, is written clearly and is understandable.

The idea of using pseudo labels for matching is a good one and will be important for training/finetuning stereo matching methods.

Experiments show that the edges can be used to obtain a small improvement over the baselines.

Weaknesses:

The paper essentially proposes additional supervision by using canny edge detection. Although this is interesting and obviously adds constraints to the network optimization, in my opinion, does not contribute enough for an ICLR submission.

The generic title on the paper is not justified by experiments solely performed on canny edges. Furthermore, I am not entirely sure how simple edge detection and matching is a physics based constraint. It would be an interesting submission for ICLR if the authors performed experiments on various edge detection/keypoint detection methods.

Several aspects of the writing can be improved, many sentences are wrongly phrased or contain typos - e.g., visual clues instead of cues.

The experimental results show that the addition of edges provides a rather small improvement, e.g., in table 2. The reason is probably that the photometric constraints with known poses are a lot stronger constraints than edges. However, one may explore the sharpness of depth around edges, which may be improved using edges.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: c.f. the weaknesses part. The paper writing can be improved a lot but the major issue possibly lies already on the problem formulation.
content.summary_of_the_review: I advise the authors to go back to the drawing board and what the current problems are for stereo matching before exploring the methods. It appears that edge matching could help some specific problems but not a general improvement of stereo matching. It is possible that other low-level constraints such as optical flow or SIFT keypoints can help stereo matching a lot more. For these reasons I am recommending a reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a physics-regularized stereo matching method by incorporating low-level structures (i.e., edges) as regularizations via multi-task learning. Specifically, a disparity aggregation module is developed to associate the cost volumes and the edges during training. Experiments show that the proposed method improves the performance of several baseline models on three benchmark datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The motivation is clear and this paper is easy to follow.
+ Ablation experiments validate the main idea of the method.

Weakness:
-	This paper shares a similar idea with EdgeStereo, this method should be included for comparison and discussion.
-	In my opinion, using edges as a regularization may inevitably introduce the risk of producing fake details on the disparity maps. How to overcome this problem? The SceneFlow dataset is relatively simple with only synthetic objects. I wonder whether Canny edges can also produce comparable accuracy as compared to GT edges on the KITTI datasets. Besides, it would be better to include learning based edge detection methods for comparison and discussion.
-	It seems the hyper-parameter gamma in Eq. (5) is critical to the performance of the proposed method. Ablation experiments should be conducted to validate the choice of this parameter.
-	As including additional information (e.g., edges) as regularizations can often improve the generalization performance, I wonder whether the proposed method can introduce consistent improvements on other datasets like ETH3D and Middlebury.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation of this paper is clear but its novelty is limited, since including edge information for stereo matching has already been studied in EdgeStereo.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the proposed method produces promising results, I have two major concerns about this paper. First, the idea of using edge information to regularize the task of stereo matching is not novel to the community. Second, the accuracy improvements of the proposed method over baselines are not significant (Table 1), especially for ACVNet.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a mechanism for improving end-to-end stereo matching networks by exploiting image edges, some of which may correspond to depth edges. The necessary edges can be obtained automatically via the Canny edge detector and can be used to improve the performance of an existing stereo matching network by adding modules to it, which can be removed in inference mode. Experiments demonstrating improved accuracy using four different underlying networks on synthetic and real datasets are also presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The edges used to regularize the network can be obtained without supervision using the Canny edge detector.

The proposed approach can be generally applied, as evidenced by results on four different stereo matching networks. The results obtained by combining ACVNet with the proposed PRNet are state-of-the-art on the KITTI benchmarks. Almost all combinations of strong baselines with PRNet lead to improved accuracy.

The additional network modules are only needed during training and can be dropped for inference. Moreover, improvements in disparity accuracy seem to be greater than what would be expected due to the increase in network capacity.

Weaknesses

The description of disparity aggregation is very hard to follow. See comments below under clarity.

Equation (5) is also not described clearly. First, the symbol p in focal loss is conditional and it is not just the probability of one of the classes. Second, it is unclear whether p is the probability of Canny or true depth edges.

The overall loss in (6) is also poorly motivated. Based on the information provided, it specifies a multi-task network estimating disparity and edgeness at each pixel. Given the lack of clarity in the presentation of disparity aggregation, it is hard to follow how these tasks interact.

Considering how the Scene Flow dataset was constructed by super-imposing foreground objects on totally unrelated backgrounds, it can be expected that the strongest edges are those between foreground and background. Validating this property on a real dataset with dense ground truth, such as the Middlebury 2014 dataset, would have been informative.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presented research is of high quality. The observation that RGB edges may indicate depth edges is clearly not novel as it dates back several decades, but the use of edges in this context is an interesting and effective idea.

The method is described with sufficient clarity to be reproducible based on the text, while the code will be made available if the paper is accepted. (Intuition is missing in certain places – see below.)

Clarity

My largest concern in terms of lack of clarity is about the way disparity aggregation is presented. I have read Sections 3.1 and 3.2 multiple times, and I still do not understand how disparities are aggregated. I understand some of the low-level details, but not how aggregation is implemented and why. Section 3.2 presents a sequence of operations and equations without much intuition. For example, the merged feature in (3) seems to be a result of feature selection via soft-max and not a result of feature merging. Then, in (4) the RGB feature is averaged with m again. The choices made by the author are validated experimentally, but some theoretical justification would have been helpful to readers, especially those engaged in similar research.


I think that the title does not shed much light on what the method actually does. “Physics-regularized” to me suggests a method taking into account gravity or similar constraints. I think that “edge-regularized/based” would have been more precise, especially since only one type of constraint is demonstrated.

The review of related work is brief, and more importantly, does not relate the publications surveyed with the proposed method.

EdgeStereo should have been compared in detail with the PRNet since it is the most related method. Also, the IJCV version of the work should have been cited.

Since PRNet included unsupervised aspects, some representative publications on unsupervised/self-supervised stereo should have been cited. Examples include:
C. Zhou, H. Zhang, X. Shen, and J. Jia, “Unsupervised learning of stereo matching,” in ICCV, 2017.
Aleotti, F., Tosi, F., Zhang, L., Poggi, M. and Mattoccia, S. Reversing the cycle: self-supervised deep stereo through enhanced monocular distillation. In ECCV, 2020.
Yang, G., Zhao, H., Shi, J., Deng, Z., Jia, J.: Segstereo: Exploiting semantic information for disparity estimation. In ECCV. 2018.
Zhong, Y., Dai, Y., Li, H.: Self-supervised learning for stereo matching with self-improving ability. In: CVPR, 2017.

The red box in Fig. 1 does not seem to generate an output that informs the rest of the network. 

The text correctly states that depth edges are often associated with RGB edges, but never clearly presents that the opposite relationship does not hold. The last sentence of Section 3.3 is the first occurrence of the fact that RGB edges do not necessarily correspond to depth edges. Do texture edge have adverse effects on disparity aggregation?

The parameters used by the Canny edge detector are not provided.


Minor Comments

Introduction, line 2: the work of Mancini et al. which is cited as an example of stereo or multi-view depth estimation actually relies on single-view depth estimation. The work of Albaija et al. is on data generation.

Introduction, first paragraph: few would argue against MC-CNN by Zbontar and LeCun as a milestone in learning-based matching cost estimation.

p. 5, 3 lines from end: “forth” should be replaced by “fourth.”
content.summary_of_the_review:
The method relies on a simple idea, the likely co-occurrence of RGB and depth edges, which is exploited effectively yielding an approach that is generally applicable and able to achieve high accuracy on widely used benchmarks. Based on the strengths listed above, I am in favor of accepting the paper. My largest concern is on lack of clarity on important aspects of the approach, as described above. 

I would like to see clarifications primarily on my comments on Section 3 in the rebuttal.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to  add a regularization framework  to existing deep learning supervised  stereo algorithms. The framework  is said  to be  "physics-based" and relies  on "low-level  structures" to provide improved performance.

The  regularization  is essentially enforcing  the preservation of the relationship between edges in the  images (or image  features), and  the final disparity map. The assumption is that edges are low-level  structures  that play an important role in  stereo matching,  so the  training should reflect this.

The  regularization module  is used during  training  only, and is said to improve the  performance of various algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The first weakness of the proposed method  is the the "physics" aspect  of  the regularization is not well justified. The paper mentions "we often observe that a large change in disparity or depth often leads to a substantial
change in intensities" as a justification, which is very thin,  especially when it is obvious that  this relationship is  not bijective (as acknowledge in the paper: "the color changes often appear in RGB images and they may not correspond to depth changes" ).

The  claim that the proposed regularization "pushes the data-driven model toward physics-driven" is not accurate, in our opinion. Supervised methods are, by  design, extremely data-driven. The proposed regularization,  even if unsupervised by  itself, does not reduce that data dependency.

Experimental results are marginally better than without the  proposed  regularization, especially  with regards to  ACVNet,  which it does not significantly improve (less than 0.1%, much  less than the error margin, I assume ).

The qualitative results (Fig 3) show a strange behavior... it seems  the  regularization makes the neural architecture learn how to recognize edges that are not relevant  to stereo matching. While the first row illustrate intended behavior  of enhanced depth map along edges, the two  subsequent rows remove specular reflections and the last row "fix" occluded regions. This suggests that the "edge enhancement" is  achieved,  but  the physical explainability is not.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The  paper is well written and clear. However, some affirmations are too broad or insufficiently justified  ("less data-driven" ,  "physics-based", "improves the model explainability").

The regularization, to our knowledge, is novel, but since it is marginally improving other well known methods, the impact of this novelty is reduced.

Technically, the paper mentions that edges is color images have a physics-based interpretation,  but it actually compute edges on features, not colors.  This should be discussed.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper falls short if its aim to provide a physics-based regularization that  significantly impact current supervised  stereo algorithms.

content.title: Physics-Regularized Stereo Matching for Depth Estimation
content.abstract: Depth estimation from stereo or multi-view images is an essential technology for a wide range of vision and robotics applications. In recent years, many deep learning based methods have been proposed for this purpose. However, training the stereo matching network is challenging and requires a large amount of data, especially for the 3D convolution networks. Existing stereo matching approaches are mostly data-driven, which often converge to a local minimum biased to the training data. In this paper, we propose a novel self-supervised physics regularization framework to improve the training of the networks using physical knowledge or constraints. More specifically, we explore the use of low-level structures as physical constraints for the regularization of the stereo-matching network via multi-task learning. Moreover, a disparity aggregation module is proposed to aggregate the disparity output with image features to consider the association in between. We also find that the canny edge can be used as a pseudo ground truth to train the network with performance comparable to the ideal ground truth edge in the Scene Flow dataset. We combine the proposed physics regularization with four existing stereo matching algorithms. The experimental results in three public datasets, including Scene Flow, KITTI 2012, and KITTI 2015, show the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework.
